cur:objects3-bradbourne-cross-crucifixio.summary: On the broken shaft of the Anglo-Saxon cross at Bradbourne, Christ hangs on the cross beneath the two discs of sun and moon, his arms outstretched along the cross-bar, while two smaller figures stand below at either side, the soldiers who bring the sponge and the spear. Weathered and patched together after being broken, it remains a moving early English image of the Crucifixion set up in the open churchyard for all to see.
facts: The cross was at some point smashed and has since been partially reconstructed in the churchyard of All Saints, a church site that goes back to Saxon times.
Sun and moon above the Cross recall the darkness at the Crucifixion and became a standard feature of early medieval Crucifixion images.
cur:objects3-bradbourne-cross-crucifixio.notes: Wikipedia describes it as an 8th-century depiction of the Crucifixion; other accounts place the cross in the early 9th century. The identification of the lower flanking figures as Stephaton and Longinus follows the usual convention.

princeton:34143.summary: On the round discus of this North African red-slip lamp stands a single frontal figure holding a long cross, flanked by the two filling holes, while a ring of small stamped motifs runs around the shoulder. Princeton identifies the figure as Christ triumphant, a victorious image that suited a lamp: the light of the flame may have recalled Christ as the light of the world. Such lamps were made in great numbers in the workshops of Roman Tunisia.
facts: The lamp is made of African red slip ware, the fine orange-red pottery of Roman North Africa, and Princeton dates it to the second half of the 5th century.
It was bought by the museum from Geledakis in Paris in August 1923.
It was lent to the 1947 Baltimore exhibition 'Early Christian and Byzantine Art' (no. 633) and shown again in 'Byzantium at Princeton' in 1986 (no. 135).
princeton:34143.notes: The figure is small and worn in the photograph; details such as beasts beneath the feet, common on this lamp type, cannot be confirmed.
